about: EC1A3 is an Autumn Term half unit in microeconomics, compulsory on a wide range of LSE programmes, including Mathematics and Economics; Mathematics, Statistics and Business; Politics and Economics; and Philosophy, Politics and Economics. It cannot be combined with EC1A5 and assumes A-level Mathematics; it is a different course from EC1A1, the Winter Term Microeconomics I course for BSc Economics students. According to the 2026/27 course guide it covers the building blocks of microeconomic analysis: rationality and individual decision-making, game theory, consumer behaviour, firms' strategic choices, how auctions work, behavioural models and individual welfare. Teaching is 20 hours of lectures and 10 hours of classes, with weekly problem sets in exam style, and assessment is a 2-hour exam (plus 15 minutes' reading time) in the January exam period worth 90% plus continuous assessment worth 10%. The optional suggested reading is Acemoglu, Laibson and List's Microeconomics, with Jacques for the maths.
topics: Building blocks: optimisation, opportunity cost and equilibrium
Game theory: strategic interaction and equilibrium

notes.h: Building blocks: how economists model choices
notes.body:
EC1A3 opens with the toolkit used in every later topic: people optimise, they face trade-offs, and outcomes are analysed as equilibria. Acemoglu, Laibson and List's Microeconomics (optional suggested reading in the 2026/27 course guide) organises the whole subject around these ideas.

Three core principles
- Optimisation: agents try to choose the best feasible option given their information and preferences.
- Equilibrium: a situation in which no agent would benefit from changing their behaviour, given what everyone else is doing.
- Empiricism: economists test models against data, ideally using comparisons that isolate cause and effect.

Scarcity and opportunity cost
- Resources (time, money, attention) are limited, so every choice involves a trade-off.
- The opportunity cost of an action is the value of the best alternative given up.
- It includes explicit costs (money paid) and implicit costs (forgone earnings, forgone leisure).
- Example: going to a free concert when your best alternative was a shift paying £60, plus £10 travel, has an opportunity cost of £70, even though the ticket is free.

Optimisation in levels and in differences
Suppose revising for h hours gives benefit B(h) = 60h − 2h² (in pounds of value), and each hour costs £20 of forgone earnings.
- In levels: compute net benefit N(h) = 60h − 2h² − 20h for each h and pick the largest. N(9) = 198, N(10) = 200, N(11) = 198, so h = 10.
- In differences (marginal analysis): keep going while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost. MB = 60 − 4h and MC = 20, so h = 10.
- Both methods give the same answer. The marginal method is usually quicker and generalises to calculus: at an interior optimum, the derivative of net benefit is zero.
- Common errors: stopping where total benefit is maximised (MB = 0, here h = 15) ignores cost; stopping where total benefit equals total cost (h = 20) throws away all the net gain.

Models
- A model is a simplified description of reality that isolates a mechanism. Assumptions are judged by whether the model explains and predicts well.
- Positive statements describe what is (testable); normative statements say what ought to be (value judgements).
- Ceteris paribus: change one thing at a time, holding others constant.

Equilibrium and markets
- In a competitive market, equilibrium is where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded; at that price no buyer or seller wants to trade a different amount.
- Comparative statics: shift one curve and compare the old and new equilibria.
- In strategic settings (game theory) equilibrium becomes Nash equilibrium: each player's choice is a best response to the others'.

Causation and evidence
- Correlation does not imply causation: omitted variables and reverse causality can create correlations.
- Randomised experiments and natural experiments provide credible comparisons. Field experiments (for example in charitable giving or pricing) are a feature of that optional suggested textbook.

Mathematical tools
The course uses A-level standard calculus: derivatives for marginal values, solving first-order conditions, and simple constrained optimisation. Jacques's Mathematics for Economics and Business is the suggested maths reference.

Exam tips: define opportunity cost precisely, show both the levels and marginal reasoning when asked to optimise, and say what the equilibrium condition is before solving for it.

This topic asks what economists mean by "rational" choice and how a rational person decides under time and risk. It sets up the benchmark that the behavioural topic later relaxes.

Rational preferences
- Completeness: for any two options A and B, the person prefers A, prefers B, or is indifferent.
- Transitivity: if A is weakly preferred to B and B to C, then A is weakly preferred to C.
- If preferences are complete and transitive (and, for infinite choice sets, continuous), they can be represented by a utility function: A is preferred to B exactly when u(A) > u(B).
- Utility is ordinal for riskless choice: only the ranking matters.
- Intransitive preferences (A over B, B over C, C over A) allow a "money pump": the person would pay a little to swap C for B, B for A, then A for C, ending where they started but poorer.

Rationality is about consistency, not selfishness
- A rational person can care about others, the environment or fairness. Rationality only requires choices consistent with stable preferences and beliefs.
- Revealed preference: if A is chosen when B was available, A is revealed preferred to B.

Sunk costs
- A sunk cost has already been incurred and cannot be recovered whatever you do now. It should not affect forward-looking decisions.
- Example: a non-refundable £40 ticket. If staying home is now worth £30 to you and going is worth £20, you should stay home. The £40 is lost either way.
- The sunk cost fallacy is continuing an activity because of past spending ("I've paid so I must go").

Decisions over time
- Money now and money later are compared using the interest rate: the present value of £X received in t years is X/(1 + r)^t. At r = 10%, £110 next year is worth £100 today.
- Exponential discounting, U = u(c0) + δu(c1) + δ²u(c2) + …, with 0 < δ < 1, gives time-consistent choices: a plan made today is still optimal when the time comes.

Decisions under risk
- Expected value EV = Σ pi xi.
- Expected utility EU = Σ pi u(xi). A risk-averse person has a concave u and prefers a sure EV to the risky prospect; the gap between EV and the certainty equivalent is the risk premium.
- Example: with u(x) = √x, a 50–50 gamble over £0 and £100 has EU = 5, so its certainty equivalent is £25, well below the EV of £50.

Information and beliefs
- Rational agents update beliefs using new information (Bayes' rule), and take account of what others' actions reveal.
- Rational ignorance: collecting information is costly, so it can be optimal not to be fully informed.

Why use rational-choice models?
- They give clear, testable predictions and a benchmark for welfare.
- Systematic departures (present bias, loss aversion, social preferences) can be built in as modifications, as later topics show.

Exam tips: when a question mentions past spending, check whether it is sunk; when it involves time or risk, write down the present value or expected utility explicitly.

notes.h: Game theory: strategic interaction and equilibrium
notes.body:
Game theory studies situations where each person's best choice depends on what others do. EC1A3 uses it for oligopoly, auctions and social behaviour, so the tools here recur throughout the course.

Elements of a game
- Players, strategies (complete plans of action) and payoffs.
- Simultaneous games are written as payoff matrices (normal form); sequential games as game trees (extensive form).

Dominance
- A strategy is strictly dominant if it gives a higher payoff than every alternative whatever the others do.
- A rational player never plays a strictly dominated strategy. Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies can solve some games.

Nash equilibrium
- A strategy profile in which each player's strategy is a best response to the others' strategies; no one can gain by deviating unilaterally.
- Method for 2×2 games: underline each player's best response to each of the opponent's strategies; cells with both payoffs underlined are pure-strategy Nash equilibria.

Classic games
- Prisoners' dilemma: payoffs (Cooperate, Cooperate) = (3, 3), (C, D) = (0, 5), (D, C) = (5, 0), (D, D) = (1, 1). Defect is dominant, so (D, D) is the unique Nash equilibrium, although both would prefer (C, C). Individual rationality does not guarantee collective efficiency. Applications: cartels, arms races, advertising.
- Coordination games: two or more pure equilibria (for example, both choose the same technology standard); the problem is which one is reached.
- Games with no pure equilibrium (matching pennies, penalty kicks) have equilibria in mixed strategies.

Mixed strategies
- A player randomises so that the opponent is indifferent between their pure strategies.
- Example: Row chooses Up or Down, Column chooses Left or Right. Row's payoffs: (U, L) = 3, (U, R) = 0, (D, L) = 0, (D, R) = 1. Column's payoffs: (U, L) = 0, (U, R) = 1, (D, L) = 1, (D, R) = 0. There is no pure equilibrium.
- Column plays L with probability q such that Row is indifferent: 3q = 1 − q, so q = 1/4.
- Row plays U with probability p such that Column is indifferent: 1 − p = p, so p = 1/2.
- Note the counter-intuitive feature: each player's mix is pinned down by the other player's payoffs.

Sequential games and backward induction
- Solve from the end: find the last mover's best choice at each node, then work backwards.
- The result is a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE): strategies form a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
- Entry game: an entrant chooses In or Out. If Out, payoffs are (0, 10) (entrant, incumbent). If In, the incumbent chooses Fight (−2, −1) or Accommodate (3, 4). Backward induction: the incumbent accommodates (4 > −1), so the entrant enters (3 > 0). SPNE: (In, Accommodate).
- (Out, Fight) is also a Nash equilibrium, but it relies on a non-credible threat: if entry happened, fighting would not be in the incumbent's interest. SPNE rules out such threats.
- Commitment (for example, building excess capacity in advance) can make a threat credible by changing payoffs.

Repeated games
- If the prisoners' dilemma is repeated indefinitely, cooperation can be sustained by strategies such as grim trigger (cooperate until the other defects, then defect forever), provided players value the future enough.
- With a known, finite number of rounds, backward induction predicts defection in every round.

Exam tips: always check for dominant strategies first, mark best responses clearly, and for sequential games state the SPNE as a full strategy for each player (including what they would do off the equilibrium path).

notes.h: Consumer behaviour: budgets, preferences and demand
notes.body:
This topic builds the demand curve from individual optimisation. EC1A3 uses the "buyer's problem" structure: what you like, what things cost, and how much you can spend.

The budget constraint
- With two goods: px·x + py·y ≤ m.
- The budget line has slope −px/py: the market rate at which you can swap y for x.
- A rise in income shifts the line out in parallel; a rise in px pivots it inwards around the y-intercept.

Preferences and indifference curves
- An indifference curve joins bundles the consumer likes equally.
- Its slope is −MRS, where MRS = MUx/MUy is the amount of y the consumer will give up for one more unit of x.
- Diminishing MRS (convex indifference curves) reflects a liking for balanced bundles.
- Special cases: perfect substitutes (straight-line indifference curves, such as two brands of bottled water) and perfect complements (L-shaped, such as left and right shoes).

The optimal choice
- Interior optimum: MRS = px/py, so MUx/px = MUy/py: the last pound spent on each good gives the same extra utility.
- Example: u = xy, m = 100, px = 2, py = 5. MRS = y/x = 2/5, so y = 0.4x. Budget: 2x + 5(0.4x) = 100, so x = 25 and y = 10. (This utility function always spends half of income on each good.)
- Perfect complements, u = min{x, y}, px = 2, py = 3, m = 100: buy equal amounts, so 5x = 100 and x = y = 20.
- Perfect substitutes: buy only the good with the higher MU per pound (a corner solution).

From choice to demand
- Varying px and tracing the optimal x gives the individual demand curve; summing horizontally over consumers gives market demand.
- Normal goods: demand rises with income. Inferior goods: demand falls with income.
- A price change has a substitution effect (the good is relatively dearer) and an income effect (purchasing power falls). For normal goods both reduce demand, so demand slopes down.

Elasticities
- Price elasticity of demand ε = (% change in quantity)/(% change in price) = (dQ/dP)(P/Q).
- Example: Q = 100 − 2P at P = 20 gives Q = 60 and ε = −2 × 20/60 ≈ −0.67, so demand is inelastic there.
- Arc (midpoint) elasticity between P = 20 and P = 30: %ΔQ = −20/50 = −40% and %ΔP = 10/25 = 40%, so ε = −1.
- Revenue rule: if demand is inelastic (|ε| < 1), a price rise increases total revenue; if elastic (|ε| > 1), it reduces revenue.
- Determinants: availability of substitutes, share of budget, time horizon, how narrowly the good is defined.
- Income elasticity (normal if positive) and cross-price elasticity (substitutes if positive, complements if negative).

Consumer surplus
- Willingness to pay for each unit is read off the demand curve.
- Consumer surplus = willingness to pay minus price paid, summed over units: the area under demand and above price.
- With Q = 100 − 2P (choke price 50) at P = 20, consumer surplus = ½ × 60 × 30 = 900.

Exam tips: write MRS = price ratio and the budget constraint as two equations in two unknowns, check whether a corner solution applies, and quote elasticities with their sign and an interpretation.

notes.h: How firms choose strategies: costs, competition and market power
notes.body:
The seller's problem mirrors the buyer's: firms choose output and prices to maximise profit, and the right choice depends on the market structure. EC1A3 then treats oligopoly as a game.

Costs
- Fixed costs do not vary with output; variable costs do. Sunk costs should be ignored in forward-looking decisions.
- Average cost AC = C(q)/q; marginal cost MC = dC/dq. MC passes through the minimum of AC and of AVC.
- Example: C(q) = 100 + q². MC = 2q, AVC = q, AC = 100/q + q. Minimum AC is where 100/q = q, so q = 10 and AC = 20.

Perfect competition
- Many firms selling an identical product; each takes the price as given.
- Profit maximisation: P = MC. With P = 40 and C = 100 + q², 2q = 40 so q = 20; revenue 800, cost 500, profit 300.
- Short run: produce if P ≥ minimum AVC (fixed costs are paid anyway).
- Long run: positive profits attract entry, which lowers the price until P = minimum AC. Here the long-run price is 20 and each firm produces 10.
- The market supply curve is the horizontal sum of firms' MC curves (above AVC) in the short run; with free entry and identical costs it is flat at minimum AC in the long run.

Monopoly
- A single seller faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, so selling an extra unit lowers the price on all units: MR < P.
- Choose Q where MR = MC, then read the price from the demand curve.
- Example: P = 120 − 2Q, MC = 40. MR = 120 − 4Q = 40 gives Q = 20 and P = 80; profit = 40 × 20 = 800. The efficient quantity (P = MC) is 40, so the deadweight loss is ½ × 40 × 20 = 400.
- Markup rule: (P − MC)/P = 1/|ε|. Market power is greater when demand is less elastic.
- Sources of market power: patents, control of key inputs, economies of scale (natural monopoly), network effects.

Price discrimination
- First degree: charge each buyer their willingness to pay. Output is efficient, but all surplus goes to the firm.
- Third degree: different prices for identifiable groups, higher where demand is less elastic.
- Example: market A has P = 100 − QA, market B has P = 60 − QB, MC = 20. Setting MR = MC in each: QA = 40, PA = 60 and QB = 20, PB = 40. A single price for both markets would be 50.
- Second degree: price varies with quantity or version (bulk discounts, economy vs business class), letting customers sort themselves.

Oligopoly as a game
- Few firms whose profits depend on each other's choices.
- Bertrand (price competition, identical products, equal constant MC): undercutting drives price down to MC with just two firms.
- Cournot (quantity competition): each chooses output as a best response to rivals' output; price lies between competitive and monopoly levels and falls as the number of firms rises.
- Collusion is a prisoners' dilemma: each firm gains by cheating on the cartel, but repeated interaction can sustain cooperation. Cartels are illegal under UK and EU competition law.
- Product differentiation softens price competition (monopolistic competition: in the long run, entry drives profits to zero but price stays above MC).
- Strategic moves: entry deterrence works only if the threat is credible (see backward induction).

Exam tips: always state the profit-maximising condition before solving, read prices off demand (not MC), and compare outcomes with the competitive benchmark to discuss welfare.

Auctions are games in which bidders compete for an object. EC1A3 uses them to apply game theory to a real market institution used for art, online advertising, government bonds and radio spectrum.

Formats
- English (ascending): price rises until one bidder remains, who pays roughly the second-highest bidder's dropout price.
- Dutch (descending): price falls until someone accepts.
- First-price sealed-bid (FPA): highest bid wins and pays its own bid.
- Second-price sealed-bid (SPA, Vickrey): highest bid wins but pays the second-highest bid.
- Strategic equivalences: Dutch is strategically equivalent to FPA (in both, you choose the price at which you would win, without learning others' bids). With private values the English auction leads to the same outcome as the SPA.

Values
- Private values: each bidder knows their own value, which does not depend on others' information (for example, a painting for personal enjoyment).
- Common values: the object is worth the same to all, but each has only an estimate (for example, oil drilling rights).

Second-price auction: bid your value
- Bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy.
- Why: your bid only determines whether you win, not what you pay. Bidding above your value risks winning at a price above your value; bidding below risks losing when you could have won at a price below your value. Bidding your value avoids both.
- Example: values 30, 50 and 80. With truthful bidding the bidder valuing 80 wins and pays 50, gaining surplus 30.

First-price auction: shade your bid
- Bidding your value guarantees zero surplus, so bidders bid below their value, trading off a higher chance of winning against a lower surplus if they win.
- With n risk-neutral bidders whose values are independently and uniformly distributed on [0, 1], the symmetric equilibrium bid is b(v) = (n − 1)v/n.
- Check for n = 2: if the rival bids half their value, bidding b wins with probability 2b, so expected payoff is (v − b)2b, maximised at b = v/2.
- More bidders mean more competition and less shading. With 3 bidders and values on [0, 100], a bidder valuing 60 bids 40.

Revenue equivalence
- If bidders are risk-neutral with independent private values from the same continuous distribution, the highest-value bidder always wins, and a bidder with the lowest possible value expects zero surplus, then all such auctions give the seller the same expected revenue.
- Example (n = 2, values uniform on [0, 1]): SPA revenue = expected lower value = 1/3; FPA revenue = expected (higher value)/2 = (2/3)/2 = 1/3.
- With n bidders, expected revenue is (n − 1)/(n + 1), so more bidders raise revenue.
- Revenue equivalence can fail with risk-averse bidders (they bid more in FPA, raising its revenue), asymmetric bidders or common values.

Reserve prices
- A reserve (minimum) price can raise expected revenue at the cost of sometimes not selling. With two bidders, values uniform on [0, 1] and a seller who values the object at 0, the revenue-maximising reserve is 1/2, raising expected revenue from 1/3 to 5/12, although there is a 1/4 chance of no sale.

The winner's curse
- In common-value auctions the winner is typically the bidder with the most optimistic estimate, so a naive winner tends to overpay.
- Rational bidders correct for this by bidding as if their estimate were the highest, shading bids more when there are more bidders.

Auctions in practice
Government spectrum auctions are a well-known application: the UK's 2000 3G auction raised about £22.5 billion. Design details (format, reserve prices, rules against collusion) matter for revenue and efficiency.

Exam tips: identify the format and value type first, state the dominant strategy or equilibrium bid function, and check revenue equivalence conditions before comparing formats.

notes.h: Behavioural models: when people depart from the standard model
notes.body:
Behavioural economics adds realistic psychology to economic models. In EC1A3 the aim is to identify systematic, predictable departures from the rational benchmark and to model them precisely enough to make predictions.

Present bias
- Quasi-hyperbolic (β–δ) preferences: U = u(c0) + β[δu(c1) + δ²u(c2) + …], with β < 1.
- Today is special: any delay from now is penalised by β, but trade-offs between two future dates are not.
- Example (β = 0.6, δ = 1): offered £100 today or £120 in a week, the person compares 100 with 0.6 × 120 = 72 and takes £100 now. Offered £100 in 52 weeks or £120 in 53 weeks, she compares 60 with 72 and waits. When week 52 arrives, she would switch: time inconsistency.
- Field evidence: DellaVigna and Malmendier (2006) found that many gym members on flat monthly contracts attended so rarely that they paid more per visit than they would have with pay-per-visit passes, consistent with over-optimism about future self-control.
- Sophisticated people seek commitment (deadlines, savings plans with penalties); naive people overestimate their future patience.

Reference dependence and loss aversion
- People evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point (status quo, expectations), and losses loom larger than gains (prospect theory, Kahneman and Tversky, 1979).
- Endowment effect: owners demand more to give up a good than non-owners will pay for it.
- Framing: logically equivalent choices described as gains or losses can lead to different decisions (Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 "Asian disease" problem).
- Status quo bias and the power of defaults follow from loss aversion and inertia.

Heuristics and biases
- Availability (judging probability by how easily examples come to mind), representativeness (judging by similarity to a stereotype, neglecting base rates), and anchoring (estimates pulled towards an arbitrary starting number).
- Overconfidence: overestimating one's own ability or the precision of one's information.
- Mental accounting (Thaler): treating money differently depending on its source or intended use, even though money is fungible.

Social preferences
- Ultimatum game: a proposer offers a split of a sum; the responder accepts (split implemented) or rejects (both get nothing).
- With purely self-interested players, the subgame perfect equilibrium has the responder accepting any positive offer, so the proposer offers (almost) nothing.
- In experiments, offers of 40–50% are common and low offers are often rejected: responders pay to punish unfairness.
- Dictator game (the responder cannot reject): many proposers still give something, showing altruism or concern for fairness, though less than in the ultimatum game.
- Models: inequality aversion, reciprocity, warm glow from giving.

How economists use these models
- Each bias is modelled with a parameter (β, a loss-aversion coefficient, a weight on others' payoffs), which can be estimated and tested.
- Behavioural models change predictions about savings, labour supply, pricing (firms may exploit biases, for example with gym contracts or add-on fees) and policy (defaults, nudges).
- Not every anomaly in the lab survives in markets with experience and high stakes, so evidence from the field matters.

Exam tips: show calculations from each decision date for present bias, contrast the SPNE prediction with experimental results for the ultimatum game, and name the specific bias rather than saying "people are irrational".

notes.h: Individual welfare: measuring how well off people are
notes.body:
The course ends by asking how economists judge whether a change makes people better or worse off. This links consumer theory to policy and to the behavioural topic.

Utility, willingness to pay and welfare
- Standard welfare economics uses preferences as the measure of welfare: if a person chooses A over B, A is taken to make them better off (revealed preference).
- Because utility is ordinal, economists measure welfare changes in money terms: how much a person would pay for, or need to be paid to accept, a change.

Consumer surplus
- Consumer surplus (CS) is the area under the demand curve and above the price: total willingness to pay minus total payment.
- A price rise reduces CS by a rectangle (extra paid on units still bought) plus a triangle (surplus lost on units no longer bought).
- Example: Q = 100 − 2P. At P = 20, Q = 60 and CS = ½ × 60 × 30 = 900. At P = 30, Q = 40 and CS = ½ × 40 × 20 = 400. The loss of 500 = rectangle 10 × 40 = 400 plus triangle ½ × 10 × 20 = 100.

Compensating and equivalent variation
These are more precise money measures (check whether your lectures use them).
- Compensating variation (CV): the income change needed after a price change to restore the original utility.
- Equivalent variation (EV): the income change at the original prices that would cause the same utility change as the price change.
- Example: u = √(xy), m = 100, py = 1; px rises from 1 to 4. The consumer spends half her income on each good, so x falls from 50 to 12.5 and utility falls from 50 to 25. Restoring utility 50 at the new prices costs 200, so CV = 100. Utility 25 at the old prices costs 50, so EV = 50. The fall in CS (area under x = 50/px between 1 and 4) is 50 ln 4 ≈ 69.3, between the two.
- For a normal good facing a price rise, EV < loss in CS < CV. With no income effects (quasi-linear utility) all three coincide, which is why CS is a good approximation when income effects are small.

Efficiency
- An allocation is Pareto efficient if no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
- A Pareto improvement makes at least one person better off and no one worse off.
- Total surplus (consumer plus producer surplus) is maximised in a competitive market without market failures; deviations (monopoly, taxes, price controls) create deadweight losses.
- Efficiency is not equity: a Pareto-efficient outcome can be very unequal. Judgements about distribution require value judgements (for example, a utilitarian sum or a Rawlsian focus on the worst-off).

Behavioural welfare economics
- If choices reflect biases (present bias, inattention, mistaken beliefs), revealed preference may not reveal welfare.
- With β–δ preferences, should welfare be judged by the present self (who values immediate gratification) or the long-run self (who wants to save and exercise)? Many economists use the long-run preferences, which supports commitment devices and default-based policies.
- Libertarian paternalism (nudges) aims to help people who are biased while imposing little cost on those who are not, for example by setting a default but allowing opt-outs.
- Critics worry that policymakers also have biases and that paternalism can override legitimate preferences.

Exam tips: compute surplus changes as clearly labelled rectangles and triangles, distinguish efficiency from fairness, and when discussing behavioural welfare, say explicitly which preferences you treat as the welfare standard.

The responder accepts any positive offer, so the proposer offers (almost) nothing.
Offers of 40–50% are common, and low offers are often rejected.
The proposer splits a sum and the recipient cannot reject; many proposers still give positive amounts.
Estimates are pulled towards an initial, possibly irrelevant, number.
Equivalent options described as gains or losses lead to different choices.
Treating money differently depending on its source or intended use, though money is fungible.
No one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
A change that makes at least one person better off and no one worse off.
Income change needed after a price change to restore the consumer's original utility.
Income change at original prices equivalent in utility terms to the price change.

cards.f: When CS, CV and EV coincide
cards.b: When there are no income effects (quasi-linear utility).
Steering choices (e.g. with defaults) while leaving people free to opt out.

questions.q: Revising for h hours gives benefit B(h) = 60h − 2h², and each hour costs £20 in forgone earnings. How many hours maximise net benefit?
questions.why: Marginal benefit 60 − 4h equals marginal cost 20 at h = 10. Fifteen hours maximises total benefit (60 − 4h = 0) but ignores the £20 cost of each hour. Twenty hours is where total benefit equals total cost (40h = 2h²), so all the net gain has been used up. Thirty hours is where the benefit itself falls back to zero.

questions.q: Your ticket to a concert is free. Your best alternative is working a shift that pays £60, and getting to the concert costs £10 in travel. What is the opportunity cost of going?
questions.why: Opportunity cost counts everything given up: the £60 forgone wage plus the £10 spent on travel. £0 looks only at the ticket price and ignores both the forgone shift and the travel. £60 counts the forgone wage but leaves out the travel cost. £10 counts only the money spent and ignores the forgone earnings.

questions.q: Using an example, explain the difference between optimisation in levels and optimisation in differences, and show that they lead to the same choice.
markScheme: Defines optimisation in levels: compare total net benefit of each option
Defines optimisation in differences: compare marginal benefit with marginal cost of each step
Works an example correctly (e.g. B = 60h − 2h², cost 20 per hour: net benefits 198, 200, 198 at h = 9, 10, 11; MB = MC at h = 10)
Explains why they agree: net benefit rises while MB > MC and falls once MB < MC
questions.modelAnswer: Optimisation in levels calculates the total net benefit of every option and picks the largest. Optimisation in differences asks, step by step, whether moving to the next option adds more benefit than cost. Example: revising h hours gives benefit 60h − 2h² and costs £20 an hour. In levels, net benefit N(h) = 40h − 2h² is 198 at h = 9, 200 at h = 10 and 198 at h = 11, so 10 hours is best. In differences, the marginal benefit of an extra hour is 60 − 4h and the marginal cost is 20, so keep revising while 60 − 4h > 20, i.e. until h = 10. They must agree because total net benefit increases exactly when marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost and decreases once it falls below, so the peak in levels is where MB = MC.

questions.q: You bought a non-refundable £40 ticket for tonight. Now you would value staying in at £30 and going out at £20 (not counting the ticket). What should a rational decision-maker do?
options: Go, unless staying in is worth more than £60
Stay in, because £30 > £20 and the £40 is sunk
Go, because otherwise the £40 is wasted
questions.why: The £40 has been spent whatever you do now, so only future benefits matter, and staying in is worth more. 'Otherwise the £40 is wasted' is the sunk cost fallacy. Adding the £40 to the value of going counts a past cost as if it were a future benefit. Requiring staying in to beat £60 also adds the sunk £40 to one side of the comparison.

questions.q: A person prefers apples to bananas, bananas to cherries, and cherries to apples. Which statement is correct?
options: Her preferences are rational as long as she makes each pairwise choice consistently
Her preferences violate transitivity, so she could be exploited by a sequence of trades
Her preferences violate completeness
Her preferences can be represented by a utility function with u(apples) > u(bananas) > u(cherries)
questions.why: Ranking A over B and B over C, yet C over A, is a cycle that violates transitivity and allows a money pump. Completeness holds, because she does rank every pair. A utility function would need u(A) > u(B) > u(C) and u(C) > u(A) at the same time, which is impossible. Consistency within each pair is not enough: rationality in the economic sense needs both completeness and transitivity.

questions.q: What do economists mean by 'rational' choice? Explain why a rational person may still give to charity, ignore sunk costs, and be risk-averse.
markScheme: Rationality as complete and transitive preferences, with choices maximising them given constraints and beliefs
Rationality does not require selfishness: preferences can include others' welfare, so giving is consistent
Sunk costs cannot be changed, so a rational choice depends only on future costs and benefits
Risk aversion is a feature of preferences (concave utility), not a failure of rationality
Notes rational-choice models provide a benchmark against which behavioural departures are measured
questions.modelAnswer: In economics, a rational person has complete and transitive preferences and chooses the best option they can afford given their information. Nothing in this definition says what people should like. A person who cares about others can rationally give to charity: the donation buys something she values, the well-being of others or the 'warm glow' of giving. Rationality does require consistency in how past and future are treated: a sunk cost has already been paid and cannot be recovered whatever she now does, so a rational choice compares only future costs and benefits and ignores it. Risk aversion is also compatible with rationality: with a concave utility of wealth, she prefers a certain amount to a gamble with the same expected value and will pay a risk premium (for example, for insurance). The rational model is useful because it gives clear predictions and a welfare benchmark, against which systematic deviations, such as the sunk cost fallacy or present bias, can be identified.

questions.q: In a 2×2 game, Row's payoffs are (Up, Left) = 3, (Up, Right) = 0, (Down, Left) = 0, (Down, Right) = 1, and Column's payoffs are (Up, Left) = 0, (Up, Right) = 1, (Down, Left) = 1, (Down, Right) = 0. In the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium, with what probability does Column play Left?
questions.why: Column must make Row indifferent: Row's payoff from Up is 3q and from Down is 1 − q, so 3q = 1 − q and q = 1/4. One-half is Row's equilibrium probability of Up, found from Column's payoffs; it mixes up whose payoffs pin down whose strategy. Three-quarters is the probability Column plays Right. One-third comes from solving 3q = 1 and leaving out the (1 − q) factor on Down's payoff.

questions.q: An entrant chooses In or Out. Out gives (entrant 0, incumbent 10). After In, the incumbent chooses Fight, giving (−2, −1), or Accommodate, giving (3, 4). What is the subgame perfect equilibrium?
options: The entrant stays out and the incumbent would fight if entry occurred
The entrant enters and the incumbent fights
There is no pure-strategy subgame perfect equilibrium
The entrant enters and the incumbent accommodates
questions.why: Backward induction: after entry the incumbent prefers Accommodate (4 > −1), so the entrant compares 3 with 0 and enters. Staying out with a threat to fight is a Nash equilibrium, but the threat is not credible, since the incumbent would not fight once entry had happened, so it is not subgame perfect. Entry followed by fighting is not even a Nash equilibrium, as the incumbent would switch to Accommodate. Finite games of perfect information always have a pure-strategy SPNE, found by backward induction.

questions.q: Using the entry game (Out gives entrant 0, incumbent 10; after In, Fight gives (−2, −1) and Accommodate gives (3, 4)), explain why (Out, Fight) is a Nash equilibrium but not a subgame perfect equilibrium. How might the incumbent make its threat credible?
markScheme: Shows (Out, Fight) is a NE: given Fight, the entrant's Out (0) beats In (−2); given Out, Fight costs the incumbent nothing (10 either way)
Explains the threat is never tested on the equilibrium path
In the subgame after entry, Fight (−1) is worse than Accommodate (4), so it is not a best response there; SPNE requires optimal play in every subgame
SPNE is (In, Accommodate)
Credibility via commitment that changes payoffs: e.g. investing in excess capacity so fighting becomes more profitable than accommodating
questions.modelAnswer: (Out, Fight) is a Nash equilibrium: if the incumbent's strategy is to fight, the entrant gets −2 from entering and 0 from staying out, so Out is a best response. Given that the entrant stays out, the incumbent's choice at the entry node never happens, so it gets 10 whatever it plans and Fight is (weakly) a best response. But the equilibrium relies on a threat that would not be carried out: in the subgame after entry the incumbent gets −1 from fighting and 4 from accommodating, so it would accommodate. Subgame perfection requires strategies to be optimal in every subgame, including those off the equilibrium path, so (Out, Fight) is ruled out and the SPNE is (In, Accommodate). To make the threat credible, the incumbent must change its own payoffs before the entrant moves, for example by investing in extra capacity that makes a price war cheaper (or accommodation costlier) so that fighting gives it more than accommodating. A visible commitment of this kind could then deter entry.

questions.q: A consumer has u = xy, income 100 and prices px = 2 and py = 5. What bundle maximises utility?
questions.why: MRS = y/x = 2/5, so y = 0.4x; substituting into 2x + 5y = 100 gives x = 25 and y = 10 (half of income on each good). Swapping to x = 10, y = 25 costs 20 + 125 = 145, more than the income, so it is not affordable. The bundle (50, 20) is the two budget-line intercepts, which spends all income on each good separately. Equal quantities of about 14.3 treat the goods as perfect complements, but u = xy allows substitution.

questions.q: Demand is Q = 100 − 2P and the price is 20. What is the point price elasticity of demand, and what happens to total revenue if price rises slightly?
options: −2; revenue falls
About −0.67; revenue rises
About −0.67; revenue falls
−1.5; revenue falls
questions.why: ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) = −2 × 20/60 ≈ −0.67. Demand is inelastic, so a price rise reduces quantity proportionally less and revenue rises. Saying revenue falls gets the revenue rule backwards for inelastic demand. The value −1.5 multiplies the inverse-demand slope dP/dQ = −0.5 by Q/P = 3, which is the reciprocal of the elasticity. The value −2 is just the slope dQ/dP, without scaling by P/Q.

questions.q: A consumer treats coffee (x) and milk (y) as perfect complements, always using them one-for-one: u = min{x, y}. Derive the demand for coffee as a function of px, py and m, and explain why a change in the price of coffee has no substitution effect.
markScheme: Optimum at the kink x = y, since extra units of one good alone add no utility
Budget: px·x + py·x = m, so x* = y* = m/(px + py)
Demand for coffee falls with both its own price and the price of milk (complements)
No substitution effect because the consumer will not substitute between goods at any price ratio; the whole price effect is an income effect
questions.modelAnswer: With u = min{x, y}, utility rises only if both goods increase together, so buying more of one without the other is wasted. The optimum is therefore at the kink of the L-shaped indifference curve, where x = y. Substituting into the budget px·x + py·y = m gives (px + py)x = m, so x* = y* = m/(px + py). Demand for coffee falls when either price rises, as expected for complements. A rise in px changes the relative price, but because the indifference curves are right-angled the consumer would still choose x = y at any price ratio: the compensated (substitution) effect is zero. The whole fall in coffee demand is an income effect, since the coffee-and-milk combination has become more expensive.

questions.q: A price-taking firm has cost C(q) = 100 + q² and the market price is 40. What are its output and profit?
options: q = 10, profit 200
q = 40, profit −100
q = 20, profit 300
q = 20, profit 400
questions.why: P = MC gives 40 = 2q, so q = 20; revenue 800 minus cost 100 + 400 = 500 leaves profit 300. A profit of 400 leaves out the fixed cost of 100. Producing 10 is where average cost is lowest, but a price-taker maximises profit where P = MC, not at minimum AC. Producing 40 sets the price equal to average variable cost (AVC = q), which is the wrong condition.

questions.q: A monopolist with marginal cost 20 sells in two separate markets: market A has demand P = 100 − QA and market B has P = 60 − QB. If it can price discriminate, what prices does it set?
options: PA = 60 and PB = 40
PA = PB = 20
PA = 40 and PB = 60
PA = PB = 50
questions.why: MR = MC in each market: 100 − 2QA = 20 gives QA = 40 and PA = 60; 60 − 2QB = 20 gives QB = 20 and PB = 40. Prices of 20 are the competitive outcome, P = MC. PA = 40 and PB = 60 swaps them, putting the higher price in market B, where demand is more elastic at these prices. A single price of 50 is the profit-maximising uniform price for the combined market (total quantity 60), which the firm can improve on by discriminating.

questions.q: In a competitive industry every firm (actual or potential) has cost C(q) = 100 + q², and market demand is Q = 1,000 − 10P. Find the long-run equilibrium price, output per firm, market output and number of firms. Explain the role of entry.
markScheme: AC = 100/q + q, minimised where 100/q = q: q = 10, AC = 20
Long-run price = minimum AC = 20 (zero economic profit)
Market output Q = 1,000 − 200 = 800
Number of firms = 800/10 = 80
Explains that profits attract entry, shifting supply out and lowering price until P = min AC; losses cause exit
questions.modelAnswer: In the long run, firms enter while profits are positive and exit while they are negative, so the equilibrium has zero economic profit and every firm producing at minimum average cost. AC = 100/q + q, which is minimised where its derivative −100/q² + 1 = 0, so q = 10 and AC = 10 + 10 = 20. (MC = 2q = 20 there too, as MC cuts AC at its minimum.) The long-run price is therefore 20. Market demand at P = 20 is 1,000 − 200 = 800, so with each firm producing 10 there are 80 firms. If the price were higher, say 40, each firm would make a profit (300 at q = 20), attracting entry; the market supply curve shifts right and the price falls until profit is driven to zero at P = 20.

questions.q: Three bidders with private values 30, 50 and 80 take part in a second-price sealed-bid auction and bid their values. What happens?
options: The bidder with value 80 wins and pays 30
The bidder with value 50 wins and pays 30
The bidder with value 80 wins and pays 50
The bidder with value 80 wins and pays 80
questions.why: The highest bid wins and pays the second-highest bid, so 80 wins and pays 50. Paying 80 applies the first-price rule. Paying 30 uses the lowest bid rather than the second-highest. The bidder valuing 50 cannot win, because there is a higher bid of 80.

questions.q: In a first-price sealed-bid auction with 3 risk-neutral bidders whose values are independently uniform on [0, 100], what does a bidder with value 60 bid in the symmetric equilibrium?
questions.why: The equilibrium bid is b(v) = (n − 1)v/n = (2/3) × 60 = 40. Bidding 60 means winning gives zero surplus, so it cannot be optimal. Bidding 30 uses the two-bidder formula v/2, ignoring the extra competition from the third bidder. Bidding 20 uses v/n instead of (n − 1)v/n.

questions.q: Explain the winner's curse. In what type of auction does it arise, and how should a rational bidder adjust their bid?
markScheme: Arises in common-value auctions where bidders have noisy estimates of the same true value
The winner is the bidder with the highest estimate, which is likely to be an overestimate
A naive bidder who bids based on their own estimate tends to overpay on average
Rational bidders bid as if their estimate is the highest (condition on winning) and shade bids down
Shading should increase with more bidders and with noisier estimates; example such as oil leases or spectrum
questions.modelAnswer: The winner's curse arises in common-value auctions, where the object is worth roughly the same to everyone but each bidder has only an imperfect estimate of that value, such as oil drilling rights or a jar of coins. Even if every estimate is right on average, the bidder who wins is the one with the highest estimate, which is likely to be too high. A bidder who bids on the basis of their own estimate alone will therefore tend to overpay when they win. A rational bidder recognises that winning is itself bad news about the value: they should ask what the object is worth given that their estimate is the highest, and shade their bid down accordingly. The correction should be larger when there are more bidders (the highest of many estimates is more biased upwards) and when estimates are noisier. Failing to make it leads to losses for winners, which is why sophisticated firms adjust bids in such auctions.

questions.q: A person has β–δ preferences with β = 0.6 and δ = 1 (per week). She is offered (i) £100 today or £120 in one week, and (ii) £100 in 52 weeks or £120 in 53 weeks. What does she choose?
options: £120 in one week in (i), but £100 in 52 weeks in (ii)
£100 today in (i), but £120 in 53 weeks in (ii)
£120 in one week in (i), and £120 in 53 weeks in (ii)
£100 today in (i), and £100 in 52 weeks in (ii)
questions.why: In (i) she compares 100 with 0.6 × 120 = 72 and takes £100 now; in (ii) both options are in the future, so she compares 0.6 × 100 = 60 with 0.6 × 120 = 72 and waits. Choosing £120 both times ignores β, which is how an exponential discounter with δ = 1 would choose. Choosing £100 in 52 weeks applies β only to the later option, but β discounts every future date relative to today. Waiting now but grabbing early in the distant choice reverses the direction of present bias.

questions.q: In an ultimatum game, a proposer offers a split of £10 and the responder accepts or rejects (rejection leaves both with nothing). Both care only about their own money, offers can be any amount, and the responder accepts when indifferent. What is the subgame perfect equilibrium?
options: The proposer offers £5 and the responder accepts
The proposer offers £0 and the responder rejects
Any split is a subgame perfect equilibrium
The proposer offers £0 and the responder accepts
questions.why: By backward induction the responder accepts any offer of £0 or more (accepting weakly beats getting nothing), so the proposer keeps everything. An offer of £5 is common in experiments, reflecting fairness concerns, but it is not the equilibrium for purely self-interested players. Rejecting £0 contradicts the stated rule that the responder accepts when indifferent. Any split can be supported as a Nash equilibrium using threats to reject low offers, but those threats are not credible, so they are not subgame perfect.

questions.q: Describe the typical experimental results from ultimatum and dictator games and explain what they suggest about people's preferences.
markScheme: States the SPNE prediction for self-interested players (responder accepts any positive offer; proposer offers almost nothing)
Ultimatum results: offers commonly 40–50%; low offers often rejected
Dictator results: many give positive amounts, but on average less than ultimatum offers
Interprets: responders sacrifice money to punish unfairness (inequality aversion or reciprocity); difference between games suggests some ultimatum generosity is strategic fear of rejection
Notes these preferences can be modelled (weights on others' payoffs) and are not irrational in the economic sense
questions.modelAnswer: In the ultimatum game a proposer splits a sum and a responder can accept or reject; rejection leaves both with nothing. If both care only about money, backward induction predicts that the responder accepts any positive offer and the proposer offers almost nothing. Experiments contradict this: offers of 40–50% are common, and low offers (say below a fifth of the pie) are frequently rejected, so responders give up money to punish what they see as unfair treatment. In the dictator game the recipient cannot reject, so self-interest predicts zero giving; yet many proposers still give something, though on average less than in the ultimatum game. Together these suggest that people care about fairness and others' payoffs (inequality aversion, reciprocity or altruism), and that part of the generosity in the ultimatum game is strategic, driven by fear of rejection. Such social preferences can be built into utility functions and are consistent with rational choice in the economic sense, since rationality requires consistent preferences, not selfish ones.

questions.q: Demand is Q = 100 − 2P. The price rises from 20 to 30. What is the change in consumer surplus?
questions.why: CS falls from ½ × 60 × 30 = 900 to ½ × 40 × 20 = 400, a loss of 500: a rectangle of 10 × 40 = 400 on units still bought plus a triangle of ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 on units no longer bought. A loss of 400 counts only the rectangle. A loss of 600 applies the price rise to the original 60 units, overstating the loss on units consumers stop buying. A loss of 100 counts only the triangle.

questions.q: Which statement correctly defines Pareto efficiency?
options: No one can be made better off without making someone else worse off
Total surplus is shared equally among everyone
Everyone is better off than in the initial allocation
The utility of the worst-off person is maximised
questions.why: Pareto efficiency means there is no remaining change that helps someone without hurting anyone. Equal sharing is about equity, and an efficient allocation can be very unequal. Making everyone better off than at the start describes a Pareto improvement from a particular starting point, not efficiency itself. Maximising the worst-off person's utility is a Rawlsian criterion for distribution, a different idea.

questions.q: Why might a person's choices not reveal what is best for them? Discuss the implications for how economists measure welfare and design policy, using present bias as an example.
markScheme: Standard welfare economics assumes choices reveal preferences and hence welfare
With present bias, choices made today conflict with those the same person makes for the future (time inconsistency), so there is no single preference ordering to respect
Must choose a welfare standard, e.g. long-run preferences, and justify it
Policy implications: commitment devices, defaults or nudges can raise welfare by the long-run standard while preserving choice
Caveats: paternalism, heterogeneity, policymakers' own biases or information limits
questions.modelAnswer: Standard welfare economics uses revealed preference: if someone chooses A over B, A is assumed to make them better off. This breaks down when choices are driven by systematic biases. With present bias (β–δ preferences), a person may sincerely plan to save or exercise next month, yet when next month arrives she postpones again. Her choices at different dates contradict each other, so there is no single set of preferences that her behaviour reveals. Economists must then decide which standard to use. A common answer is the long-run preferences, those she expresses when choosing for the future, because they are not distorted by the pull of immediate gratification. By that standard, under-saving is a welfare loss, and policies such as pension auto-enrolment, commitment savings accounts or other nudges can raise welfare while leaving people free to opt out. There are caveats: people differ, and a default that helps the biased may cost those who genuinely prefer to consume now; policymakers may also lack information or have their own biases, and overriding choices raises concerns about paternalism.

questions.q:
Two firms, A and B, each decide whether to Advertise or Not advertise. Payoffs (A, B) are: both Advertise (4, 4); A Advertises and B does Not (10, 2); A does Not and B Advertises (2, 10); neither advertises (8, 8).
(a) Find each firm's dominant strategy and the Nash equilibrium. Explain why this game is a prisoners' dilemma. [5]
(b) The game is repeated infinitely often and each firm discounts future payoffs by δ per period. Both firms use a grim trigger strategy: do not advertise until the other advertises, then advertise forever. Find the values of δ for which this sustains no advertising. [7]
(c) Now consider a market-entry game: an entrant chooses In or Out; Out gives (entrant 0, incumbent 10). After In, the incumbent chooses Fight (−2, −1) or Accommodate (3, 4). Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria and the subgame perfect equilibrium, and explain the difference. [7]
(d) In a different game, Row's payoffs are (Up, Left) 3, (Up, Right) 0, (Down, Left) 0, (Down, Right) 1, and Column's are (Up, Left) 0, (Up, Right) 1, (Down, Left) 1, (Down, Right) 0. Show there is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium and find the mixed-strategy equilibrium. [6]
markScheme: (a) Advertise is dominant for each (10 > 8 and 4 > 2); NE (Advertise, Advertise) with (4, 4)
(a) PD: both would be better off at (Not, Not) = (8, 8), but each has an incentive to deviate
(b) Cooperation value 8/(1 − δ); deviation value 10 + 4δ/(1 − δ)
(b) Condition 8 ≥ 10(1 − δ) + 4δ, so δ ≥ 1/3
(c) NE: (In, Accommodate) and (Out, Fight); SPNE: (In, Accommodate) by backward induction; Fight is a non-credible threat
(d) Checks all four cells for profitable deviations
(d) Column plays Left with q: 3q = 1 − q, q = 1/4; Row plays Up with p: 1 − p = p, p = 1/2
(d) Explains each player's mix makes the other indifferent
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For A: if B advertises, Advertise gives 4 and Not gives 2; if B does not, Advertise gives 10 and Not gives 8. Advertising is strictly better either way, so it is dominant. B's payoffs are symmetric, so Advertise is dominant for B too. The unique Nash equilibrium is (Advertise, Advertise) with payoffs (4, 4). It is a prisoners' dilemma because both firms would be better off at (Not, Not) with (8, 8), but each has a private incentive to deviate to Advertise, so individual rationality leads to a collectively worse outcome (for example, advertising that merely steals customers from the rival).

(b) If both follow grim trigger, neither advertises and each gets 8 every period: 8 + 8δ + 8δ² + … = 8/(1 − δ). A firm that deviates gets 10 now, after which the rival advertises forever and the best response is also to advertise, giving 4 each period: 10 + 4δ/(1 − δ). Cooperation is sustained if 8/(1 − δ) ≥ 10 + 4δ/(1 − δ). Multiplying by (1 − δ): 8 ≥ 10(1 − δ) + 4δ = 10 − 6δ, so 6δ ≥ 2 and δ ≥ 1/3. Firms that are patient enough value the future stream of 8 more than the one-off gain of 2.

(c) Nash equilibria: (In, Accommodate) — given Accommodate, entering gives 3 > 0; given entry, accommodating gives 4 > −1. (Out, Fight) — given Fight, entering gives −2 < 0 so Out is a best response; given Out, the incumbent gets 10 whatever its plan, so Fight is a weak best response. (In, Fight) is not an equilibrium because the incumbent would switch to Accommodate, and (Out, Accommodate) is not because the entrant would switch to In. Subgame perfection: in the subgame after entry the incumbent accommodates (4 > −1), so the entrant enters (3 > 0); the SPNE is (In, Accommodate). (Out, Fight) relies on a threat that the incumbent would not carry out if tested, so it fails subgame perfection.

(d) (Up, Left): Column gets 0 and would switch to Right (1). (Up, Right): Row gets 0 and would switch to Down (1). (Down, Right): Column gets 0 and would switch to Left (1). (Down, Left): Row gets 0 and would switch to Up (3). So there is no pure-strategy equilibrium. Let Column play Left with probability q. Row's expected payoff from Up is 3q and from Down is 1 − q; Row is willing to mix only if 3q = 1 − q, so q = 1/4. Let Row play Up with probability p. Column's payoff from Left is 0·p + 1·(1 − p) = 1 − p and from Right is 1·p + 0 = p; indifference requires p = 1/2. The mixed equilibrium is Row: Up with probability 1/2; Column: Left with probability 1/4. Each player's mix is set by the other player's payoffs, so that the other is willing to randomise.

questions.q:
A seller (who values the object at 0) auctions a single object to two risk-neutral bidders whose values are independently and uniformly distributed on [0, 1].
(a) Explain why bidding one's true value is a weakly dominant strategy in a second-price sealed-bid auction. [6]
(b) In a first-price sealed-bid auction, show that b(v) = v/2 is a symmetric equilibrium bidding strategy. [6]
(c) Compare the seller's expected revenue in the two auctions and relate your answer to the revenue equivalence theorem, stating its conditions. [6]
(d) Explain how a reserve price might affect expected revenue and efficiency, and discuss one reason why revenue equivalence may fail in practice. [7]
markScheme: (a) Price paid is set by the other bid, not one's own; the bid only affects whether one wins
(a) Overbidding can only add wins at prices above value (losses); underbidding can only lose profitable wins; so bidding v is weakly dominant
(b) If rival bids v/2, a bid b wins with probability P(vj/2 < b) = 2b (for b ≤ 1/2)
(b) Maximises (v − b)2b: first-order condition 2v − 4b = 0, so b = v/2
(c) SPA revenue = E[min(v1, v2)] = 1/3; FPA revenue = E[max]/2 = (2/3)/2 = 1/3
(c) Revenue equivalence conditions: risk neutrality, independent private values from the same distribution, highest value wins, lowest type gets zero surplus
(d) Reserve price raises revenue (optimal 1/2 gives 5/12) but risks no sale (probability 1/4) when values exceed seller's value: efficiency loss
(d) Failure: risk aversion raises FPA bids, or common values/winner's curse, asymmetries, collusion
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) In a second-price auction a bidder's own bid determines only whether she wins; if she wins, she pays the highest rival bid, which she does not control. Let her value be v and the highest rival bid be p. If she bids v, she wins exactly when p < v and gains v − p > 0, and loses when p > v, where winning would have meant a loss. Bidding above v changes the outcome only when v < p < bid: she now wins but pays p > v, a loss. Bidding below v changes the outcome only when bid < p < v: she now loses a win that would have given v − p > 0. So deviating from v can never help and sometimes hurts: bidding one's value is weakly dominant.

(b) Suppose the rival bids vj/2, with vj uniform on [0, 1], so the rival's bid is uniform on [0, 1/2]. A bidder with value v who bids b ≤ 1/2 wins with probability P(vj/2 < b) = P(vj < 2b) = 2b. Expected payoff = (v − b) × 2b = 2vb − 2b². The first-order condition 2v − 4b = 0 gives b = v/2 (the second derivative −4 confirms a maximum, and bids above 1/2 are never worthwhile). So the best response to the rival bidding half their value is to bid half your own value: b(v) = v/2 is a symmetric equilibrium.

(c) In the SPA with truthful bidding the price is the lower of the two values; the expected minimum of two independent U[0, 1] draws is 1/3. In the FPA the winner pays half the higher value; the expected maximum is 2/3, so expected revenue is 1/3. The revenues are equal, as the revenue equivalence theorem predicts: if bidders are risk-neutral, have independent private values from the same continuous distribution, the bidder with the highest value always wins, and a bidder with the lowest possible value expects zero surplus, all such auction formats give the same expected revenue. Bidders shade in the FPA, but they pay their own (higher) bid when they win, and the two effects exactly offset.

(d) A reserve price r means the object is sold only if a bid reaches r. It can raise revenue by forcing high-value bidders to pay at least r when the rival's value is low. With two U[0, 1] bidders and a seller who values the object at 0, the revenue-maximising reserve is 1/2, raising expected revenue from 1/3 to 5/12. The cost is efficiency: with probability 1/4 both values are below 1/2 and the object goes unsold, although it is worth more to a bidder than to the seller. Revenue equivalence can fail in practice. If bidders are risk-averse, they bid more aggressively in the FPA (to reduce the risk of losing), so the FPA raises more than the SPA. With common values, bidders also learn about the value from others' behaviour, and fear of the winner's curse affects formats differently; asymmetric bidders or collusion can also break equivalence. This is why auction design, for example in government spectrum sales, pays close attention to format and reserve prices.
